text: It began on a Wednesday afternoon as a late December sun was just dipping below the Mumbai skyline.
Down where the elevated highway curves between glass towers, the city exhaled in horns and heat.
On the B.K.C. overpass, one city became many cities — each trapped inside its own small metal shell.
...Beneath gentle curls of raven hair, her eyes stayed fixed on distant city lights while her thoughts drifted like cigarette smoke.
Beyond the mortal clouds, in a place where endings are drafted like memos, something unprecedented was happening.
It was around that time that the girl from the window at the party was falling through the air — two floors down and fast approaching the ground.
Just as she hit the ground, Mrs. Shah was in the Amravati Hospital squeezing her husband's hand with such strength that he was screaming louder than her.
As the midwife urged her into one last push, a new life came into being. A beautiful thing that would go on to be the cause of much consternation in his many years to come.
A deal was being struck — the kind that bends the fabric of everything.
She woke up in a body that felt borrowed, in a room that smelled of antiseptic and second chances.
The neo-natal ward held its breath. Death held a baby.
And in Mumbai, even at that late hour, great thundering wheels of commerce rolled on unfettered.
And so, only a few minutes away from midnight, Laila Starr met her death once again.
Eight years later, the sun rose anyway — as it always has, as it always will.
